newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian troops ready for PNG conflict escalation.
newsitem.headline: Australian troops ready for PNG conflict escalation.

text.p: Australian Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer said on Sunday that the Australian defence forces had been placed on a higher degree of readiness because of the political crisis in Papua New Guinea (PNG).
However, he again declined to comment on whether Australia would send troops to PNG as a peacekeeping force.

"We can't go into the details of private discussions that many of us have been having with senior officials and political figures in Papua New Guinea," Downer said in a television interview when asked if Australian forces would be sent to PNG.

"I can really only say in relation to the Australian defence force that there has been some upgrading of its level of readiness, but that is of course just a natural precaution, an understandable precaution, for the Australian government to take," he said. About 10,000 Australians live in PNG.

Newspapers reported that the PNG government had formally requested that Australia send troops to PNG after self-proclaimed army leader Major Walter Enuma on Saturday again ordered Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan to resign by next Tuesday.
Major Enuma said the defence forces remained loyal to sacked army commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, and threatened confrontation if any attempts were made to disarm them.
"The impression I get is that General Singirok has the significant support of the Papua New Guinea defence force," Downer said.
"(But) we have no reason to believe at this stage that General Singirok is taking a view that the constitution shouldn't be kept in place and upheld," he said.
Downer said it appeared that some calm had returned to the capital of Port Moresby after two days of street violence last week, but he said the level of background tension remained high.

"The situation on the ground in Port Moresby is, as of this morning, now fairly calm, although I make the point so that people understand very clearly the background to that is a fairly high degree of tension," he said.
The PNG crisis began last Monday when Singirok demanded that Chan quit over his hiring of about 70 foreign mercenaries to help quell the nine-year secessionist rebellion on Bougainville Island.
Singirok was promptly fired and replaced by Colonel Alfred Aikung. Singirok's supporters, led by Enuma, have demanded that the former commander be given back his job.
Enuma said troops would return to normal duties if Singirok was reinstated or his chief of staff, Colonel Jack Tuat, was appointed acting commander.
